searchText: And I am sorry, that may decentivise theft of keys if its for finaincial gain, but not if the point is to compromise the network! Hi MIcah, thanks for your reply I understand you are a busy Dev here, but in the spirit of Ethereum, what you say is not true, the system is in a beta phase, it evolves as time goes on, you cannot seriously say that if an issue is identified the foundation wont find a fix, there is a fix, you allow a way for withdrawals to be made server side if it is needed, you dont have to force that on everyone, do you not think if it was possible the only people to use the server side option would be the good guys, I mean seriously, we're not talking 5k or 10k, we're talking hundreds of £100s it is grand theft, Ethereum has a duty to protect its investors, whether it is permissionless or not, what yuor suggesting is the key holder has no authority over his key or node, sorry but that makes no sense to me. Please work on a solution 🙏 And if this is to become a recurring issue which I guarantee it will, why not allow people to add Identity details to the contract if they so wish, why cant a client ID themselves? We are legit business people not money launderers Sorry to keep going on, please understand I am not having a go at you or any other Dev, but I disagree with the viewpoint and your explanation, I do not have a verbal contract, I have a full on digital trail, in my case there is no way the bad actor can prove he is the owner, not unless he can also hack my DNS and my paypal and banking system and ID at coinbase. Also my host knows I was conned because the conman then tried to pretend to be me to withdraw the funds and they knew straight away it wasnt me because they knew I would never have asked the questions the bad actor asked, they sent me screen shots of the conversation, the conman tried to con us both at the same time. Please ETH Devs, think this out more, while I am concerned of course for my finances, imagine some entity wants ETH 2.0 to fail, are you fully prepared for that. Please watch Cyber Polygon 2021, they warn that all IT systems may be breached. ALL, its no joke they are seriously concerned! Yes I asked my host if they were insured and they said no, they have $2B assets and no insurance, can you belive that, its madness I think it does prove ownership, and someone else may think it doesn't. The real problem is that someone has to set a line in "what constitutes proof of ownership" and there's no infallible way to do this, so we settle for "I have the private key". I do hope though that we eventually find a way to have a social manual intervention in these manners. Even though it seems theoretically impossible I can 100% prove my ownership and I can gaurantee my host knows their clients because they use email registration, and CC and Paypal payment details. Just as Coinbase and exchanges use KYC, no bad actor can prove these points. The point is, for arguments sake, if two people have the same key, then lock the node and let them go to court over it, if the host cannot identify the client, let it go to court, there is no way in a million years some Nigerian guy with a stolen key could ever prove ownership of my nodes, I have far too much evidence to prove its mine, everything is recorded digitally. Potuz, youve been very kind and understanding and given me hope via DM as have my host, I pray EF takes this issue seriously because it will happen over and over again, and it could damage the rep of Ethereum or worse damage the network, I wish you all a good night. ❤️ The most logical way was to add some identity details to the contract, yes I admit I dont know what I am on about with Blockchain, but never in my life have a signed a contract that does not have my name and signature on it. Really sorry to go on, I am in awe of the project I really am. GN, will switch off Discord now so I dont spam the hell out of the board, I was just grateful people were still discussing my issue. Thanks everyone. ❤️ True! Users can opt into smart contract wallets with social recovery. That way you don't need a universal line, each user picks their own notion of proof of ownership. Vitalik is in favour of social recovery wallets too, but very few actually building and experimenting with them <@876973674564030504> next time you can consider using a multisig or SSV if you aren't confident of custodying your own keys and would rather split ownership of the key with someone else. Why not just initially allow a holder of the withdrawal key to only withdraw to the address that made the deposit, for a limited time? Say a week or something like that. Then open up withdrawals to any address. That is an interesting idea. If your original deposit source address is compromised, but your withdraw keys are not, then you simply don't queue up until a week later. If your withdraw keys are compromised but your deposit source address is not then you queue your withdraw right away. Still an open question whether it is worth the code complexity or not. We have to be mindful that building a system that only protects one person is probably not worth the cost to the system overall due to increased complexity. Yeah I am not sure how difficult it would be to implement, but it is obviously more complex. Who knows how many keys have been compromised though? It might give many stakers some peace of mind. I think the major complication is that the beacon chain has no idea where the original deposit came from so can't verify it. It's not included in the deposit contract records or event logs so you actually have to do a bunch of chain data analysis to work out where it came from which I suspect would require a full archive node or at least transaction trace data which isn't normally stored. Block explorers make it look like it's easy to get this data but it actually really isn't. Hmm yeah I know Zapper tracks it but I imagine they are chain data wizards I actually quite like this idea. So it goes like this at withdrawal: 1) You initiate withdrawal 2) The withdrawal process waits x number of blocks to ensure there are no additional conflicting withdrawal requests to different addresses 3) At the end of the period if there is only one requested withdrawal address the validator is exited and funds transferred. If not the validator continues and keys are locked until a court makes a decision. The interesting bit is we build a smart contract for legal purposes and that is the only way to unlock the keys. The only difficulty then becomes defining who "the courts" are. But if that challenge could be overcome then the problem is mostly solved. I mean, what are the chances your attacker would even show up in court? The good thing about this is it solves multiple issues. If you never had your keys compromised you are unaffected. If you did but you didn't realise then when the attacker tries to exit you send your own exit request to block it. If you try to exit to the wrong address by mistake you have a window to try again and then explain in court what happened. And devs never need to get involved in legal issues of ownership best left to the courts, who in turn would not have any mechanism to get involved unless a conflict exists. Personally I think that any withdrawal mechanism that is designed should incorporate a grace period to listen for conflicting withdrawal requests IN CASE it is decided to do something about it. Even if it is only to identify how widespread the issue is. From a logical point of view I hate the idea that the fastest to get the message out should get the funds. "Compromised keys" is a condition that can be tested for, even if we don't want to do anything about it. > until a court makes a decision This is the part that doesn't align well with the ethos of Ethereum. I appreciate that We should still test for the condition Just adding the power for *someone* to make a decision as to who gets some money is a huge departure from the entire system's design. At the moment, noone anywhere in the system has that power, and this is very intentional. Adding code always increases complexity. If we have no intention of actually using that code then we should avoid adding it because it increases costs to the system. This case differs slightly because a change later when the intention arises could not retroactively test for the condition. I wonder what the code cost would be to just wait x blocks after a withdrawal request in case of other requests from the same keys. If another is received invalidate both requests? That way they could at least battle it out until someone gives up or there's a code change. And also we would know it's happening. And those requests are going to have a cost, attackers aren't going to want to keep paying that on risk. It's a compromise that again doesn't affect anyone whose keys have not been compromised, (other than a short wait when they withdraw,) throws a lifeline to those whose keys have been compromised whether they knew it or not, doesn't involve third party trust and measures the scope of the issue. 🤷‍♂️ It even serves as a mechanism for cancelling a withdrawal request during the grace period if you change your mind. "Conflicting withdrawal request during grace period invalidates both requests" This should probably also be slashable. Imo simplest is burn the ETH if two conflicting requests. As you say, deters people from wanting to steal keys in the first place. I can easily see people accidentally burning themselves with such a feature though. Like you initiate a withdraw and forget, then initiate another. Either way you have to test for the condition with a grace period Or you initiate a withdraw and don't understand that withdraws aren't instant so you withdraw again thinking something went wrong. That wouldn't be a conflict invalidating both requests rather than burning would be safer though Can the client warn you? "This validator has already requested withdrawal to 0xABC, your request will conflict with this one and risks burning the ETH" It could, but that is more code that needs to be written and tested and ensured to be robust. I can't speak to how *much* more code in this case, or how complex it would be given current client architecture. Maybe <#595721451651465227> but I'm also wondering if there's a way to do this for all addresses on ethereum. Burn seems better than race condition or PGA. Makes sense Dear emptymind, I am grateful that you are considering ways around this situation, this is my point, if a key was breached or stolen, the bad actor could not prove it was theirs in court, & as you say more than likely would NOT show up in court becuase they would probably go to jail once the judge realised the person was a thief, but why can EF not create an option A: where the the server side key & withdrawal key can be used together to initiate an option to block external withdrawals & make withdrawals possible only from the server side . Lee Sutton explained to me before this could create an issue with the host, but if this can only be activated with both keys, whats the issue? If the host is having difficulty identifying the rightful owner then phase B: is initiated where the node stays locked until the rightful owner is identified, this achieves multiple things, 1: gives the host and key holder a chance to work together or resolve the issue in court, 2 it gives the rightful owner a chance to get legal ownership of the node back, 3 locking the node means the network doesnt have a withdrawal making the network stronger and doesnt burn the ETH which is a bad idea anyway sorry, 4 it mitigates any resentment from investors who get robbed who most likely will initiate court cases because we could be talking serious sums of money at the point of withdrawal, & lastly 5 it protects the reputation of EF. To me it is unthinkable that EF would turn a blind eye to fraud within the POS network, especially to investors that basically helped launc

excerpts.author: potuz
excerpts.content: I think this idea shouldn't be dismissed just yet: we can put the onus on proving the deposit on the caller. Perhaps the caller can provide whatever information is needed to verify the transaction and the original 20 bytes address from which it originated. Then consensus engine will just forward this directly to the execution engine to verify it before scheduling the withdrawal. If this is feasible then we can also mitigate the engineering complexity by giving it low priority and putting the onus on providing the respective PRs on the affected wallets by either directly coding or financing devs to do it.

Sadly Potuz, my specfic issue, I lost the key to the node and the wallet I made the transaction from, but the ETH was originally transferred to my cold air gapped wallet from my acccount on Coinbase so I could get that verified as they use KYC. I have just sent an email to the CEO of my host, I would like to ask to what extent they have breached keys, how common or rare it is, the other problem is some may not know the keys have been breached, I dont quite understand how the CLI setup works, but does it create a log on the computer with sensitive infrmation that can be hacked?

I know I am a nobody, but in my tiny brain, I still think a way for a key holder to work with the host, where the withdrawal key holder authorises the host to block external withdrawals and then the two parties can work together stress free to either withdraw and setup a new node, or just leave the node running if there is no fear for an external threat is the best option. If I had to, I would travel to California from Europe so we both input the keys at the same time to inistiate the withdrawal, this option does not have to affect any users, only those who are uncertain if their key were breached or sure they were, it gives the key holders a chance to resolve a breach, learn from their mistakes, and with luck, continue to be part of this exciting project protecting the Ethereum base layer, the more the ETH increases in value the harder it will be for people like me to be involved in securing the network, so for a decentralised point of view, protecting the little guys does makes sense.

If my host tried to screw or blackmail me I would sue them, I just cannot see that ever happeing, my host for example has $2B value of nodes, I am sure they would never consider hurting their customers or reputation, my understanding is they are prepared to go to great lengths to protect us.

Sorry to put my awe in again, over and out.
